questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Minor in a 3x3 Matrix With Variable Entries
questions.problem:
What is the minor of ${k}_{22}$ in the matrix
$K=[\begin{aligned}p & p & -p \\ -q & q & q \\ q & -2 & q\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we remove the second row and the second column:

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}p & ∗ & -p \\ ∗ & q & ∗ \\ q & ∗ & q\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Next, we calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}p & -p \\ q & q\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}p & -p \\ q & q\end{aligned}| \\  & =p\cdot p-q\cdot (-p) \\  & =pq+pq \\  & =2pq\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Minor in a 3x3 Matrix With Variable Entries

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function
questions.problem: The population $p$, in millions, of a particular colony of bacteria after $t$ days can be modeled by the function $p(t)=\frac{{2}^{{t}^{2}+1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the bacteria population as a function of $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the bacteria population is equal to ${p}^{′}(t).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{2}^{{t}^{2}+1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot (2t)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =2t\cdot {2}^{{t}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Expressions in Degrees Using the Sum and Difference Formulas
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the difference formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v={210}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{210}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{210}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{210}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Simplifying Expressions in Degrees Using the Sum and Difference Formulas

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression Using the Secant-Tangent Identity: Replacing a Squared Secant
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x
$$

We rewrite the given expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2\,{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x} & =\frac{2\,(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)-1}{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{2+2{tan}^{2}⁡x-1}{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x}{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x}}{\cancel{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x}=1.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Simplifying an Expression Using the Secant-Tangent Identity: Replacing a Squared Secant

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & ={9}^{5-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{5-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{5-x}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x=(5-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(5-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Center and Lengths of the Major and Minor Axes Given the Equation of an Ellipse
questions.problem: What is the center of the ellipse $\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-6)^{2}}{36}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have $h=-4$ and $k=6,$ so the center is located at $(-4,6).$

provenance.kp_title: Determining the Center and Lengths of the Major and Minor Axes Given the Equation of an Ellipse

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum to Infinity of a Geometric Series Given Two of Its Terms
questions.problem: Consider the infinite geometric sequence that has a fourth term equal to $24$ and a seventh term equal to $\frac{3}{8}.$ What is the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence?
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{4}=24$ and ${a}_{7}=\frac{3}{8}.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{7-4} & =\frac{(\frac{3}{8})}{24} \\ {r}^{3} & =(\frac{3}{8})(\frac{1}{24}) \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{1}{64} \\ {r}^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{4})}^{3} \\ r & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}
$$

for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence, we can find the first term. Indeed, for $n=4$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}(r)^{3} \\ 24 & ={a}_{1}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3} \\ 24 & ={a}_{1}(\frac{1}{64}) \\ {a}_{1} & =1\,536\end{aligned}
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1\,536}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{1\,536}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =1\,536(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =2\,048.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Sum to Infinity of a Geometric Series Given Two of Its Terms

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve
questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{2}-1,\,y=4{t}^{5}+1$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=20{t}^{4}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{20{t}^{4}}{2t}=10{t}^{3}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(10{t}^{3})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{30{t}^{2}}{2t} \\  & =15t.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve
